questions.question: How many heading levels are there, and what is the rule for heading order?
questions.answer: h1 through h6. Use them to build a logical outline without skipping levels; h1 is the page topic, h2 sections, h3 subsections. Never pick a level for its default size — style with CSS.

questions.question: What is the difference between strong/b and em/i?
questions.answer: strong marks importance and em marks stress emphasis, both meaningful to assistive tech. b and i apply bold/italic styling without extra semantic meaning, for brand names or alternate tone.

questions.question: When should you use pre, blockquote, q, and hr?
questions.answer: pre preserves whitespace and line breaks for code or ASCII art. blockquote is a long quotation from another source, q a short inline quote with automatic quotes, and hr a thematic break between sections.

questions.question: What do time, data, address, and dfn represent?
questions.answer: time marks a machine-readable date/time via datetime, data pairs visible text with a machine value, address holds contact details for the nearest article or page, and dfn marks the defining instance of a term.

questions.question: Why is using h4 right after h1 a problem even if it looks right?
questions.answer: It breaks the document outline that screen readers and search engines use to navigate. Visual size should come from CSS; heading level should reflect structural depth, so use h2 next.

questions.question:
Why should you not use

or empty

tags for spacing?
questions.answer: They inject meaningless nodes and styling into the content, break responsive spacing, and are announced oddly by assistive tech. Use CSS margins or layout containers instead.
